title: Building semantic models on the gold layer
summary: Designing a semantic model over gold marts: entities, join paths, grain safety, time spines, a worked MetricFlow and Snowflake example, and testing.

blocks.text: 36.1 Start from the gold marts

A semantic model is only as good as the tables beneath it. Build it on gold marts (chapter 15) with a declared grain, stable keys and conformed dimensions, not on silver tables or raw sources. Our running example is a retail gold layer:
Write the grain of every gold table in its description and test it (a uniqueness test on the grain key). The semantic layer trusts that grain to decide how to join and aggregate safely.
36.2 Entities and join paths

Entities are the join keys of the semantic graph. For each table decide which entity is *primary* (one row per value) and which are *foreign* (many rows per value). Safe joins go from the many side to the one side: `fct_orders` to `dim_customers` via `customer`, `fct_order_lines` to `fct_orders` via `order`.

blocks.title: Join graph of the example
blocks.text:
fct_order_lines --order--> fct_orders --customer--> dim_customers
        |                                                 ^
        +--product--> dim_products                        |
  fct_support_tickets -------------customer---------------+
  arrows: many-to-one (safe direction for joining dimensions)

items: Prefer one path between two entities. Two paths (for example customer via order and via a shipping address table) make results ambiguous.
Role-playing dimensions (order date, ship date) need distinct names, not one ambiguous `date`.
Keep entity names business-friendly and identical across models: `customer` everywhere, not `cust` in one model.

blocks.text: 36.3 Grain safety: fan-out and chasm traps
Two classic errors produce plausible but inflated numbers.

items: **Fan-out trap**: joining a one-side table to its many side and then summing a one-side measure. Joining `fct_orders` to `fct_order_lines` and summing `shipping_fee` counts each order's fee once per line.
**Chasm trap**: two facts that both relate to a dimension but not to each other. Joining orders and tickets through customer multiplies rows: a customer with 3 orders and 4 tickets yields 12 rows.

blocks.title: Chasm trap and the fix
blocks.text:
-- WRONG: revenue inflated by ticket count
SELECT c.region, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue, COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS tickets
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN fct_support_tickets t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.region;

-- RIGHT: aggregate each fact to the target grain, then join
WITH o AS (SELECT c.region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
           FROM fct_orders f JOIN dim_customers c USING (customer_id)
           GROUP BY c.region),
     t AS (SELECT c.region, COUNT(*) AS tickets
           FROM fct_support_tickets f JOIN dim_customers c USING (customer_id)
           GROUP BY c.region)
SELECT COALESCE(o.region, t.region) AS region, o.revenue, t.tickets
FROM o FULL OUTER JOIN t ON o.region = t.region;

Good semantic engines generate the second pattern automatically: each measure is aggregated within its own model, then results are joined on the requested dimensions. That is the main reason to let the layer write SQL rather than users.
36.4 Time spines

Cumulative metrics, offsets (*vs last month*) and gap-filling need a calendar with one row per period, even for days without orders. In MetricFlow this is a **time spine** model; newer dbt versions configure it in YAML. Check the current documentation for your version, as this configuration has changed.

blocks.title: Time spine declaration (dbt)
blocks.text:
models:
  - name: time_spine_daily
    time_spine:
      standard_granularity_column: date_day
    columns:
      - name: date_day
        granularity: day
36.5 The worked example in MetricFlow

blocks.title: models/semantic/sales.yml

blocks.text: A query for `revenue` and `average_order_value` grouped by `customer__region` and `metric_time__month` joins orders to customers along the many-to-one path. Note that `average_order_value` here divides paid revenue by all orders; whether the denominator should also be filtered is a business decision to write down, not an accident of SQL.
36.6 The same model as a Snowflake semantic view

blocks.title: Snowflake semantic view (sketch)
blocks.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE SEMANTIC VIEW analytics.sales_sv
  TABLES (
    orders AS analytics.fct_orders PRIMARY KEY (order_id),
    customers AS analytics.dim_customers PRIMARY KEY (customer_id)
  )
  RELATIONSHIPS (
    orders_to_customers AS orders (customer_id) REFERENCES customers
  )
  FACTS (
    orders.order_amount AS amount,
    orders.paid_amount AS CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN amount END
  )
  DIMENSIONS (
    orders.order_date AS order_date,
    orders.status AS status,
    customers.region AS region
  )
  METRICS (
    orders.revenue AS SUM(orders.paid_amount),
    orders.order_count AS COUNT(orders.order_id)
  )
  COMMENT = 'Sales metrics on gold marts';

SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(
  analytics.sales_sv
  DIMENSIONS customers.region
  METRICS orders.revenue, orders.order_count
);

Semantic views are a fast-moving Snowflake feature. The clause structure above follows the documented pattern (TABLES, RELATIONSHIPS, FACTS, DIMENSIONS, METRICS), but verify syntax, synonyms, derived metrics and query options against the current documentation before relying on them.
36.7 Testing, versioning and ownership

items: **Reconciliation tests**: for each certified metric, compare semantic-layer output with a hand-written SQL query on gold for a fixed period. Run in CI.
**Validation**: run the tool's config validation in CI (for example `mf validate-configs` in open-source MetricFlow) to catch broken references and ambiguous joins.
**Snapshot tests on key numbers**: last closed month's revenue should not change after a deploy unless the change is intended and announced.
**Versioning**: changing a definition is a breaking change for consumers. Publish `net_revenue_v2` alongside the old metric, migrate dashboards, then deprecate.
**Ownership**: each metric has an owning team (finance owns revenue, product owns activation), a certification status and a description written for business users.

blocks.title: Certifying revenue for the board
blocks.text: A retailer's finance and analytics engineering teams agreed a definition of net revenue (paid orders minus refunds, excluding tax, by payment date). They encoded it as a metric, added a reconciliation test against the ledger within 0.1% per month, and marked it certified.
items: Dashboards switched from custom SQL to the metric.
A later change of refund timing shipped as `net_revenue_v2` with a two-month overlap.

blocks.title: Extend the semantic model
blocks.text: Add product-level analysis to the example: revenue by category and units sold, using `fct_order_lines` and `dim_products`. Decide which semantic models, entities and measures you need, where fan-out could occur with order-level measures such as `shipping_fee`, and how you would test the new metrics.
hints: Should category revenue come from order lines or orders?
Which existing metric could silently change if joins are added carelessly?

items: Build semantic models on gold marts with declared, tested grain.
Entities define join paths; join from many to one and keep a single path between entities.
Fan-out and chasm traps inflate numbers; aggregate each fact at its own grain, then join.
Time spines enable cumulative, offset and gap-filled metrics.
Test metrics by reconciliation and snapshots, version breaking definition changes, assign team ownership.

blocks.q: Summing order-level shipping_fee after joining orders to order lines causes what?
options: No error, because SUM is additive
A fan-out trap that counts each fee once per line
blocks.explain: Joining to the many side repeats order rows per line, so an order-level measure is multiplied. A chasm trap involves two unrelated facts joined through a shared dimension.

blocks.q: Orders and support tickets are both joined to customers in one query. A customer has 3 orders and 4 tickets. How many joined rows does that customer produce?
blocks.explain: Without pre-aggregation every order pairs with every ticket: 3 x 4 = 12. This chasm trap is why semantic engines aggregate each fact separately before joining.

blocks.q: Why does a revenue growth metric with offset_window need a time spine?
options: To store revenue in a separate table
To provide a complete calendar so periods without orders still exist for offsets and gap-filling
blocks.explain: Offsets and cumulative windows join to a continuous calendar; missing days would break comparisons. The spine does not store revenue.

blocks.q: Finance changes the refund timing rule for net revenue. What is the safest rollout?
options: Remove the metric until the change is agreed
Edit the existing metric in place and redeploy
Ask each dashboard owner to update their SQL
Publish a new versioned metric alongside the old one, migrate consumers, then deprecate
blocks.explain: Changing a certified definition in place silently changes historical numbers. Versioning lets consumers migrate deliberately with an overlap period.
